newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pill's path to approval in Japan still uncertain.
newsitem.headline: Pill's path to approval in Japan still uncertain.

text.p: The low-dose contraceptive pill has cleared the first hurdle in its latest bid for official approval in Japan, but analysts with memories of government turnarounds say a 30-year struggle is by no means over.
A government report presented to a special Health Ministry committee this week declared the low-dose birth control pill safe and effective, fueling expectations it could be legalised this year.
Currently in Japan, only some kinds of middle-dose and high-dose pills are permitted for the treatment of menstrual disorders.
Hopes were initially fanned last year when the then-Health Minister said he expected the government report to come out in favour of the pill.
But with another two government panels, at the least, required to give their blessing, officials and activists say approval is not yet assured.
"We don't deny the possibility that it might be approved this year but it is hardly definite," a Health Ministry official said. "At this stage, it will still take some time."
Yuriko Ashino, deputy executive secretary of the Family Planning Association said that while she had high hopes for this year, the outlook was "still grey".
"It's gotten through stage one but stage two and stage three are going to be tough. Its a positive step but that doesn't mean it will be approved," she said.

The pill, introduced in the West in the 1960s, has had a long and tortuous passage through numerous Japanese government committees. Concerns over sexual mores, side effects, AIDS, as well as public indifference, have all played their part in keeping it off the market.

In late 1995, hopes for approval were again raised here, only to be dashed when officials were sent scurrying back into discussion over a scare in Europe that some brands of current "third-generation pills" carried a greater risk of blood clots.
"We've been down this sort of road before and the Health Ministry's basic stance is still very cautious," said Ashino.

Lingering concerns about AIDS are seen as the main obstacle to approval but some industry observers suggest that resistance from Japanese doctors against drugs not covered by insurance, was also a factor.

"The pill is unlikely to be covered by insurance and Japanese doctors in general oppose the introduction of uninsured drugs, ones that won't be reimbursed," said Shigeru Mishima, a pharmaceuticals analyst at UBS Securities.
Nine companies have applied to distribute the pill, most of them Japanese firms with tie-ups with Western manufacturers.
"Any one company would be lucky to capture 10 percent of the market," Mishima said.

Shares in German drug maker Schering AG, a major manufacturer of contraceptive pills, rose over four percent on Wednesday on the news of the government report. However a Schering spokeswoman said one estimate of the potential Japanese market at $818 million was overdone.

"The market is not that big. I put it at around 36 billion yen ($300 million) a year," said Mishima, adding that surveys showed less than ten percent of Japanese women had expressed interest in the pill.
A spokesman for major Japanese drugmaker Yamanouchi Pharmaceutical, which plans to offer the Schering-brand pill under licence, said it was practically impossible to measure the size of the market.
"It depends on what sort of pricing it will take, how much women's consciousness has changed in Japan -- its too hard to tell," he said.

On prospects for approval this year, the Yamanouchi spokesman said, "In short, we really don't know. The authorities haven't said anything to us and it seems as if the debate about its safety and effectiveness will still go on." ($=120)
